title: Non-Euclidean Gradient Descent Operates at the Edge of Stability
claim: Under gradient descent, curvature measures rise until they plateau at the stability threshold set by the step size, even as the loss keeps falling.
layout: 2x4 grid of line plots; columns are metrics, rows are architectures; dotted threshold lines
description: A 2x4 grid of training-curve line plots. The top row is an MLP and the bottom row is a CNN. The columns are Train Loss (grays), Gradient Norm (reds), Directional Smoothness (greens) and Sharpness (blues). Each panel shows three curves for three step sizes η, with darker shades for larger η. The x-axis is iterations, up to 3×10^4. Train loss falls smoothly. Gradient norm is noisy and non-monotonic. In the directional smoothness and sharpness columns, the curves rise (sharpness rises gradually, directional smoothness jumps) and then level off at horizontal dotted black lines. These lines mark the 2/η thresholds, for example 50, 100 and 200. The eye goes first to the plateaus pinned at the dotted lines in the right-hand columns. Legends in each panel list the η values.
caption: Vanilla GD on CIFAR-10-5k. Top: MLP; bottom: CNN. Columns show train loss, gradient norm, directional smoothness, and standard ℓ2 sharpness. Dashed lines mark the stability threshold 2/η.
abstract: The Edge of Stability (EoS) is a phenomenon where the sharpness (largest eigenvalue) of the Hessian approaches and then hovers near the stability threshold $2/Î·$ during gradient descent (GD) with step size $Î·$. Despite (apparently) violating classical smoothness assumptions, EoS has been widely observed in deep learning, but its theoretical foundations remain incomplete. We provide an interpretation of EoS through the lens of Directional Smoothness [Mishkin et al., 2024]. This interpretation naturally extends to non-Euclidean norms, which we use to define generalized sharpness under an arbitrary norm. Our generalized sharpness measure includes previously studied vanilla GD and preconditioned GD as special cases, as well as methods for which EoS has not been studied, such as $\ell_{\infty}$-descent, Block CD, Spectral GD, and their normalized versions. Through experiments on neural networks, we show that non-Euclidean GD with our generalized sharpness also exhibits progressive sharpening followed by oscillations around or above the threshold $2/Î·$. Practically, our framework provides a geometry-aware spectral diagnostic that can be applied across a broad class of non-Euclidean gradient methods.
